windows.region: South Africa (general, SAAGA industry overview)

source.quote: the South African avocado season extended from February to October, but with new plantings at higher elevations and more southerly latitudes harvesting now takes place from February in the to mid-January.
source.doc: SA Avocado Industry Overview – South African Avocado Growers' Association (SAAGA)

windows.region: South Africa - warm subtropical regions (Hass cultivar)

source.quote: Hass ... Flowering and harvesting months ... Warm regions ... Flowering: July - September ... Harvesting: June - October
source.doc: Directorate Communication: Cultivation of Avocados (South African Dept. of Agriculture / ARC-Institute for Tropical and Subtropical Crops)

windows.region: South Africa - cool subtropical regions (Hass cultivar)

source.quote: Hass ... Cool regions ... Flowering: August - October ... Harvesting: August - December
source.doc: Directorate Communication: Cultivation of Avocados (South African Dept. of Agriculture / ARC-Institute for Tropical and Subtropical Crops)

source.quote: Hass was the most precocious cultivar, with bearing starting in the second season, and reaching 10 t ha-1 by year three.
source.doc: Wolstenholme, Kaiser & Palmer, 'Yield Potential of Intensively Managed Avocados in the Natal Midlands — The Early Bearing Years', South African Avocado Growers' Association Yearbook 1991, 14:15-18

yearsToFirstCrop.note: Bruyns Hill, Natal Midlands bioclimatic group 2; irrigated Hass on clonal Duke 7 rootstock, 7 x 7 m (200 trees/ha), planted 1982–1984. The paper reports Hass starting in its second season and Fuerte in its third. The two-to-three-year reference describes those trial cultivars, not every avocado or nursery starting age.

source.quote: Hass was the most precocious and consistent bearer, averaging over 15 t ha-1 and reaching an average of 20 t ha-1 by the sixth year. Thereafter, an average yield of about 22,5 t ha-1 appears to be sustainable.
source.doc: Wolstenholme, Kaiser & Palmer, SAAGA Yearbook 1991, 14:15-18

yearsToFullBearing.note: In this irrigated, intensively managed Natal Midlands trial, Hass reached about 20 t/ha at age 6 and orchards approached maximum sustainable average yield by age 8. This is a trial-specific bearing reference; there is no national plateau or automatically interpolated age-yield curve.

source.quote: reaching an average of 20 t ha-1 by the sixth year. Thereafter, an average yield of about 22,5 t ha-1 appears to be sustainable ... At a spacing of 7 x 7 m (200 trees per ha)
source.doc: Wolstenholme, Kaiser & Palmer, SAAGA Yearbook 1991, 14:15-18

yieldKgPerTree.note: Same-trial arithmetic at the initial 200 trees/ha: 20,000 kg/ha / 200 = 100 kg/tree at age 6; sustainable average 22,500 kg/ha / 200 = 112.5 kg/tree. At age 3, 10,000 kg/ha / 200 = 50 kg/tree equivalent. These are average-equivalent reference values for the named Hass/Duke 7 orchard conditions, not measured individual-tree yields or default production for a different density, cultivar, climate or management. Intermediate ages are not inferred.

source.quote: Hass, an A-type flowerer, tended to be out of phase with Fuerte and Rinton on a seasonal yield basis ... favourable temperatures at fruit-set (especially in B flowering type cultivars such as Fuerte) can result in heavy cropping
source.doc: Wolstenholme, Kaiser & Palmer, SAAGA Yearbook 1991, 14:15-18

pollination.note: SA source confirms avocado's type A / type B protogynous dichogamous flowering system (temporal separation of male and female phases within a single tree) rather than stating self-fertility directly. Supporting SA quote on the practical effect: DAFF/ARC 'Cultivation of Avocados' guide lists for Fuerte (a Type B cultivar) 'Comments: fruit set increased by a pollinator' (http://www.avocadosource.com/international/south_africa_papers/cultivation_of_avocados.pdf, p.5), i.e. trees do set fruit alone (self-fertile) but cross-pollination with the opposite flower type improves fruit set — hence 'partly-self-fertile' rather than 'self-fertile' or 'needs-cross-pollinator'.

supplementaryReferences.title: Hass age benchmarks — irrigated Natal Midlands trial

source.quote: 10 t ha-1 by year three
source.doc: Wolstenholme, Kaiser & Palmer (1991), SAAGA Yearbook 14:15–18; reflowed PDF

supplementaryReferences.note: Hass on Duke 7, initially 200 trees/ha at Bruyns Hill (Natal Midlands bioclimatic group 2), with intensive irrigation and nutrition. Age 3: 10,000 kg/ha; age 6: 20,000 kg/ha; sustainable average about 22,500 kg/ha. Same-study density permits equivalents of 50 kg/tree at age 3 and 100 kg/tree at age 6; there is no reference for every intermediate age. These orchard benchmarks are conditional on good resources, comparable climate and timely orchard management, including Phytophthora control and thinning; do not auto-fill farm quantities.

source.quote: In pecans [Carya illinoinensis (Wangenh. K. Koch)], male (staminate) and female (pistillate) flowers occur on the same tree (monoecious) and exhibits heterodichogamy ... Therefore, trees were divided into two groups: “Protandrous” (Type I) which is when pollen from the male flowers is shed before the female flowers are receptive, and “Protogynous” (Type II), where female flowers are receptive to pollen before pollen is shed from the male flowers ... Compatible cultivars need to be in close proximity to each other for successful cross-pollination ... It is possible for fruit to set through self-pollination in the case of incomplete dichogamy, but this often results in smaller and lighter nuts ... Under self-pollination, pecan yield is 35 – 75% lower with nut quality severely reduced (Polles et al., 1980). Complete dichogamy will result in a self-sterile cultivar, as there is no overlap between pollen shed and pistil receptivity.
source.doc: Lötze, E., 'Literature Review: Factors influencing pollination of pecans for commercial production', published by SAPPA

pollination.note: Pecan is wind-pollinated and monoecious (male and female flowers on the same tree) but exhibits heterodichogamy — male and female flowers on a given tree mature at different times (Type I protandrous vs Type II protogynous) — so a single tree/cultivar alone generally cannot pollinate itself well or at all (many named cultivars are effectively self-sterile), and commercial orchards in South Africa are planted with complementary Type I x Type II cultivar combinations. Self-pollination is possible in some cultivars with incomplete dichogamy but yields 35-75% less with poorer nut quality — hence 'needs-cross-pollinator' rather than 'partly-self-fertile' or 'self-fertile'.

source.quote: Cross-pollination increases yields by 52% when compared with open pollination. ... Cross-pollination increases yields by 48.5% and improves nut quality (size and kernel weight). ... Genotyping of macadamia kernel to determine pollen parents: A4 was highly outcrossing (97%), 695 was 64% outcrossed, 816 41% outcrossed and 814 showed 10% outcrossing. ... Results demonstrated the critical role of honeybee colonies in macadamia orchards, with the absence of bees resulting in only 30% production in both cultivars.
source.doc: SAMAC (South African Macadamia Growers' Association), 'What have we learned 2024' research summary newsletter

pollination.note: Changed from needs-cross-pollinator to partly-self-fertile in editor review: the same SAMAC summary measures 10-97% outcrossing by kernel genotyping (so some nuts are selfed) and says cross-pollination RAISES yield by about half, which is a partly self-fertile tree, not one that needs a pollinator to bear. SAMAC's own research summaries show macadamia is capable of self/open pollination (a cultivar-dependent 10-97% outcrossing rate was measured by kernel genotyping, and orchards without managed bee colonies still achieved 30% of full production) but that yield is substantially higher (48.5-52% more) with cross-pollination (interplanted cultivars) and managed honeybee colonies (industry recommends at least two hives/ha). This mixed picture — fruit set possible alone, but commercially reliant on cross-pollination/bee activity — is why 'needs-cross-pollinator' (the industry-recommended practice) rather than 'self-fertile' was chosen, though 'partly-self-fertile' is also defensible given the cultivar-dependent self/open-pollination yield floor; see this nuance rather than treating the choice as clear-cut.

source.quote: Bees are the principal pollinators. There is some self- and cross-incompatibility but several cultivars have set fair crops of seedless or few-seeded fruit.
